# The Prophetic Poet: Jeremiah 17

- Author: Daniel Lira Serhan (https://danielliraserhan-rgb.github.io/)
- Type: Exegetical paper
- Course: 5313 Hermeneutics · Dallas Baptist University
- Date: 2024-11-11
- URL: https://danielliraserhan-rgb.github.io/ensayos/the-prophetic-poet/
- PDF: https://danielliraserhan-rgb.github.io/ensayos/the-prophetic-poet.pdf
- Language: en

*Full text of the paper, reproduced exactly as in the original document.*

---

**The Prophetic Poet**

Daniel Lira Serhan

Class 5313: Hermeneutics

November 11, 2024

STRUCTURAL DIAGRAM AND OUTLINE FOR TEACH

Thus says *Adonai*:

“Cursed is

> the one who trusts in man,

> and depends on flesh as his arm,

> and whose heart turns from *Adonai*.

> For he will be like a bush in the desert.

> He cannot see goodness when it comes,

> but will dwell in parched places

> in the wilderness—

> a salt land where no one lives.

Blessed is the one who trusts in *Adonai*,

> whose confidence is in *Adonai*.

> For he will be like a tree

> Planted by the waters,

> spreading out its roots by a stream.

> It has no fear when heat comes,

> but its leaves will be green.

> It does not worry in a year of drought,

> nor depart from yielding fruit.

“The heart is deceitful above all things,

and incurable—who can know it?

I *Adonai*

search the heart,

I try the mind,

> to give every man according to his ways,

> according to the fruit of his deeds.

Like the partridge that gathers a brood that she did not hatch,

> so is he who gets riches but not by justice;

> in the midst of his days they will leave him,

> and at his end he will be a fool.

A glorious throne

> set on high from the beginning

> is the place of our sanctuary.

O Lord,

the hope of Israel,

> all who forsake you

> shall be put to shame;

> those who turn away from you

> shall be written in the earth,

> for they have forsaken the Lord,

the fountain of living water.

OUTLINE

1. *The past:* Eco of the garden  
*Answers the question: Why is the world the way it is? How did we get here?*

a. Curses

i. Trust in man \[a\]

1. Like a bush in the desert \[b\]

b. Blessings

i. Trust in Adonai \[a\]

1. Like a tree in waters \[b\]

2. *The present:* The heart of God vs heart of Man   
*Answers the question: Why does faith in man produce a curse?*

a. Heart of man \[a\]

i. Deceitful

ii. Only God can search the heart of man

b. Heart of God \[a\]

i. Fair, Just,

ii. Gives according to what they deserve

3. *The future:* Fruit of men vs fruit of God.   
*Answers the question: Where does the road end*

a. Weirdly placed proverb

i. The man tried to get riches by the Tree of Knowledge \[b\]

1. A brood that they did not hatch

2. Good at first, but lonely at last

ii. God has set a place \[b\]

1. A throne since the beginning

a. Echoes the past, calling for faith in the present

2. As a place of our sanctuary

a. Points to. The future calling for rest in the present

4. *The way:* The real mikveh  
*Answers the question: How do we get there?*

a. The hope of Israel \[a\]

i. Play of words with the cleaning mechanism, Mikveh

1. Only by placing our hope, honor, loyalty, and faith in Israel

b. Contrast by: \[a\]

i. Those who forsake vs those who honor

ii. Those who turn away vs those who turn back

c. The fountain of living water \[a\]

i. Ends with the same play of words: Mikveh

1. Not only the living water

a. The fountain of living water.

**Introduction**

Was he really the weeping prophet or just an incredible poet? According to the author of this paper, Jeremiah has been wrongly deemed the weeping prophet, at least within the Mexican church. Jeremiah is the author of the deepest poems, drawing from the depths of the wells of The Word to give Israel and the body of believers a drink of revelation. Jeremiah links proven theological truths with their origins, bringing them to his present time and projecting them to the future hope. He paints a beautiful canvas for everyone’s mind and heart that gets deeply entangled with our souls. It is impossible for the avid reader not to pounder on the glorious wisdom, sanctity, justness, and goodness of God once they finish any poem, writing, or oracle from Jeremiah’s book

By exegeting Jeremiah 17:5-13[^1], this paper will show how, through poetic, prophetic literature, Jeremiah weaves God's story together and presents it by contrasting trust in God, the heart of God, and fruit of God vis a vis trust in man, the heart of man and the fruit of Man. Specifically, this paper will show how (1) Jeremiah poetically plays with words (Adam, Curse – Blessings, arm – seed, bush – tree, wilderness – waters) to echo the events in the garden, explaining humanity's condition. Then, (2) he uses it as a mechanism to contrast the heart of men vis a vis the heart of God so (3) the reader can analyze the fruit given by both, calling them back to the garden, the place prepared for them since the beginning. Finally, (4) Jeremiah uses a play on words on the term Mikveh to show that the only way back (and forward) is through God, The Only Hope, The Cleanser, and The Spring of Living Water.

## **Historical Context**

More than a book, the commonly called Book of Jeremiah is an anthology of poems, oracles, proverbs, and narratives written by Jeremiah. He was called before adulthood, somewhere between infancy and adolescence.[^2] Called “to uproot and to tear down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant” (Jer 1:10), to be a prophet to the nations, beginning with Isreal and Judah and expounding to other nations later. [^3] He began prophesying in a transitional moment when the fall of King Ashurbanipal signaled the disintegration of the Assyrian empire, breaking the yoke of nearly a century. [^4] He continues through Josiah’s kingship with the hope of the new reforms.[^5] Instead, he watched how the apparent reform and renewed national power did not penetrate the hearts of Judah and died with King Josiah.[^6] Eventually foreseeing and seeing the advance of Babylonia in the hands of King Nebuchadnezzar who would take Juday captive and exile for 70 years. [^7]

His message highly intertwines his personality with history and profound wisdom about God's character, will, and works. Jeremiah abounds in using poetic literature to recall profound truths found in the Pentateuch, especially the book of Deuteronomy, whose influence is notable in its content.[^8] Jeremiah is a true poet who expresses, according to this author, the words of Moses in Deuteronomy 29, forth telling the curses that will come because Israel abandoned God in exile. Still, he also grabs from Deuteronomy 30, forth telling the blessings of returning so that God can circumcise their hearts. According to Steven Smith, “*Jeremiah is about hope provided by judgment.”* [^9]  A paradoxical statement that enlightens the personality of Jeremiah and his literary style. This tragic figure finds hope in despair, determination in angst, and triumph in defeat. This makes him a true prophet, finding only in God his strength and refuge; in his decrease, God increases.[^10]

### **Literary Context**

The exegeted text in this paper is found within the first 20 chapters of the Book, which contain the main collection of prophesies and poems from Jeremiah, followed by a historical narrative intertwined with other poems and oracles.[^11] These poems and oracles are a subsection of the first section identified by Mark Dever as “Justice for God’s People (Chapters 1–45; 52)”[^12] This justice, as noted above, is part of the hope provided by judgment, a judgment that comes from the breaking of the Covenant made on Mt Sinai and renewed before entering Cannan according to Deuteronomy. [^13] As such, the consequences of the broken covenant become the major theme of Jeremiah’s book, alternating between the just-coming judgment and its renewed promise of a circumcised heart.

Understanding the heavy influence of the Deuteronomic covenant renewal is crucial to understanding how Jeremiah weaves God's story together with his writings, poems, and oracles.  The proclamation of the broken covenant, the call to return, and the eventual exile are not new information but a commentary on the Book of Deuteronomy for Judah and Israel in Jeremiah´s days. Jeremiah links the covenants of God, points to the judgment because of the broken Sinaitic covenant, and recalls the promise of the circumcision of the heart in what we first learn to be, by the oracle of Jeremiah, the new covenant. According to James Stuart Bell

> The best-known passage in Jeremiah is the new covenant text in 31:31–34. Not only is it the largest OT text quoted in the NT (Heb 8:8–12; 10:16–17), but arguably better than any other passage, it links God’s ancient promises to Eve (Gn 3:15), Abraham (Gn 12:1–3), and David (2Sm 7:16–19) with NT assurances that God in Christ grants believers new hearts, salvation, and fellowship with him.[^14]

This paper intends to show how Jeremiah uses poetic language and wisdom parallelisms to merge the message of God and present it to his contemporary audience, intended to produce repentance and the return to God by following His will, whatever it may be. The literary proposition of this paper is that Jeremiah 17:5-13 parallels Genesis 3 while bringing forth Deuteronomy 29 and 30, weaving in Psalms and Proverbs, and using a cultural understanding of Leviticus cleansing rituals (mikveh) to make a call to repentance and return to faith in God and his future promises.

### **Explanation of the Text (6 pages)**

For the explanation of the text, the author proposes an outline derived by the personal learnings of the teaching of Dr. Brent Thomasson and the authors William W Kleon, Graig L. Bloomerg, and Robert L Hubbard through their book *Introduction to Biblical Interpretation.*[^15] Said outline is described through the description of four sections in Jer. 17:5-13 and later shown in the process of exegeting text verse by verse.

Jer. 17:5-13 can be broken into four sections. The first three (Jer 17:5-12) are a series of antithetical parallelisms that work together as a Synthetic parallelism, each one adding to the contrast between men and God. The first section (Jer 17:5-8) poetically transports the reader into the past, into the garden, as a foundation to remind its readers why the world is the way it is and how they are now in a place of judgment. To do so, Jeremiah uses antithetical parallelism to contrast trust in man vis a vis trust in God by comparing them to a bush in a wilderness and a tree planted by the waters.

A technical Hebrew analysis, highlighting the parallel words and structures, is needed to demonstrate this poetic structure. The author of this paper performed this technical analysis using Logos Bible Software and Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance.

Jer 17:5 opens with the words: “Thus says Adonai,” a common phrase used by the prophets when proclaiming an oracle. Even though it may be just another use of a normal phrase in prophetic literature, combined with the whole text, it echoes the garden when Adonai first says the word Cursed (אָרַר) ʾârar in Gen. 3:14. <sup>Day</sup>[^16] This sets the poetic assonance in motion, recalling to the reader’s mind the time in the garden when the serpent was cursed. The Hebrew word curse has the same sounds as the word describing the serpent, shrewd, (עָרוּם) *ʿārûm.* In turn, the word curse has the same root as the word for naked עָרוֹם (*ʿārôm*) [^17] in Gen. 2:25, which becomes linked directly to the shame felt by Adam and his wife when they first saw.[^18]

Jer. 17:5 opens by transporting the minds of its readers to the garden, reminding them of the first time humanity fell and the pronounced curse. This curse resulted from men taking the fruit of the Tree of Knowledge. The wording intentionally echoes the garden and compares the curse placed on the serpent to the curse placed on “the one that trusts in man *(אָדָם ʾâdâm´).*[^19]

Jeremiah continues the verse with two synthetic statements describing this type of person. (1) **The one that trusts in** *(אָדָם ʾâdâm´)* depends on flesh as his arm-seed (זְרוֹעַ) *z*<sup>*e*</sup>*rôwaʿ* [^20]  A word clearly selected by Jeremiah to remember the seed (זְרֹע) *z*<sup>*e*</sup>*rôaʿ* of Genesis 3:15 that would crush the head of the serpent. Jeremiah builds it further and describes (2) how **trusting in the seed (***z*<sup>*e*</sup>*rôwaʿ* **) of men** equals turning their hearts from Adonai.[^21] Thus, it could be concluded that Jeremiah grabs from Gen. 3:14-15 and makes a poetic commentary. **The one who trusts in man** is like the one who abandoned faith in the seed promised by God to trust their own flesh; they will receive the same fate as the serpent did, a curse of nakedness and shame.

In Jer. 17:6, within the first section of the outline presented, Jeremiah builds and deepens this echo using a simile to compare **the one who trusts in man** to a bush in the desert. The word bush (עַרעָר) *ʿarʿâr* is derived from עָרוֹם (*ʿārôm*); naked.[^22] and sounds just like the word cursed (אָרַר) ʾârar*.* The use of this very specific word links, once again, **the one who trusts in men** to the curse, shrewdness, and nakedness, all fruits of sin produced by the seed of man, or in the case of Gen. 3:15, the serpent. According to Robert Jamieson, other commentators further explain the use of the word bush in the desert as a juniper tree found in the Arabah, a plant “excluded from religious uses, because it has neither fruit nor seed and is neither sown nor planted.”[^23]

What Adam and his wife intended to happen was for them to see good and evil and become like God, but instead, they received a bare plant, a naked shame, a tree with no seed or fruit. Jeremiah comments on this idea by explaining what this bush in the desert means: He cannot see goodness when it comes. Adam trusted in the serpent, and the serpent planted a seed that gave the fruit of nakedness and shame. They took from the fruit of the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil, but they cannot see it when goodness comes. Even when their “eyes are opened,” their hearts are corrupted, and they cannot see it. Just like Adam and his wife, Cain, and Seth’s descendants, the man was sent to the wilderness, a salty land where no one lives.

As an antithetical parallelism, Jer 17:7 presents **the one who trusts in Adonai** as blessed בָרַךְ bârak.[^24] The words curses and blessings, coupled together, are a core theme of the Torah and the center of prophetic commentary. Jeremiah is now relating these words to the decision made in the garden. Man either chooses to trust in Adonai or chooses to trust in the flesh. At the same time, most commentaries agree with Steven Smith in that the passage immediately brings to mind Psalm 1. The blessed man is like a tree that is “planted beside flowing streams.”[^25] Jeremiah intends to bring all Ps. 1 into the mind of his audience, showing again two paths to follow: “For Adonai knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked leads to ruin” (Ps. 1:6). Why would Jeremiah do this? For one, to show his audience the right direction, but secondly, knowing that the exile was coming, to fill those who trust Adonai with hope. The drought (exile) is coming, but those who trust in Adonai do not worry but yield fruit in every season (Jer 17:8), its leaves never drop (Ps.1:4), and it has no fear when heat comes (Jer 17:8).

The second section (Jer 17:9-10) is a synthetical parallelism of the first one; it repeats the same idea but adds more information. It is meant to answer the question: why does faith in man produce a curse, and why trust in God is better? It is important to highlight that the first section speaks of someone who trusts in man, while the second section speaks about every man’s heart condition, making it personal. This brings the principles laid in the first section into the reader’s present condition with another antithetical parallelism contrasting the **heart of man** vis a vis the **heart of God.**

Jer. 17:9 is a direct statement to pierce readers' hearts. There is no escape; every man's heart is deceitful, and this deceit has no cure. Why is it that one should not trust his own heart? We cannot even know our own hearts. [^26] It is deceitful and incurable, impossible to be known even by the enlightened gurus. No pursuit of wisdom will ever understand the heart of man. So, what, is a man then condemned to be cursed because of an incurable heart? Jer 17:10 is the most beautiful antithetical statement ever made: “I Adonai search the heart.” Adonai and Him alone is just and fair because he knows **the heart of man**. He searches the depths of the heart and only He can truly give according to what they deserve. **The heart of God** is pure, deliberate, just, noble and honest. Christopher Wright explains the beauty of this expression:

> The opening word, I, is emphatic. It seems to be a deliberate riposte to the despairing question, Who can understand it? ‘I can,’ says God, ‘I the Lord, the searcher of the heart, the examiner of the inner being.’ We may be a mystery to ourselves, but we are no mystery to the One who sees into the deepest recesses of human motives and thoughts.[^27]

The third section (Jer 17:11-12) closes the synthetical parallelism of both previous sections. While the first drives the reader to the past and the second drives the reader to the present, the third drives the reader to the future, answering the question: where would the road end if one follows each path? This is achieved by an antithetical parallelism contrasting the fruit that each would give if followed, the fruit of man vis a vis the fruit of God. The poetic mechanism to do so is an interesting metaphor in the form of a proverb: partridge that hatches eggs that are not hers. The fruit of those who trust in man is just like the juniper tree; it fields no fruit and has no seed. Like a Patridge that has no seed and hatches another bird’s eggs, whatever hatches will eventually fly away and once more leave the partridge deserted. [^28]  The fruit of man is temporal satisfaction followed by long-lasting solitude. Christopher Wright asserts that this prover is a condensed form of the theology of Psalm 73. [^29] If so, this would answer the question: What should a man do? Trust in Adonai and be confident in His heart and His ways. Even when it seems the wicked are bearing fruit, its seed bears no fruit; enter the sanctuary of God and perceive the end (Ps. 73:17).

In short, be patient and aim for eternal destiny: “A throne of glory, set up on high from the beginning, is the place of our Sanctuary (Ps. 17:12).” As Steven Smith says: Our trust is in God and his Word because our hearts are fixed on the coming reality of seeing the throne of the God who judges all.[^30] A coming reality that was set up since the beginning, the sanctuary, the consecrated place where God will tabernacle with man. From the beginning, the garden was set up to be this place, but the trust in flesh corrupted it. All three sections taken together work as a synonymous parallelism of Genesis 3 when Adam and his wife had to choose between two trees, two wills, and two fruits. This is the real choice being communicated by Jeremiah, on one hand following the path of Adam (man) and on the other following God’s plan. As Christopher Wright would say,

> “This is someone who has known the living God but who is now governing the essential core of their life (heart) without reference to God. On the other hand (7) is the person who trusts in the Lord, whose confidence is in him. The contrast is then presented in matching pictures of a stunted bush in the wastelands (6) and a tree planted by the water (8).[^31]

**The fruit of man** is corruption and leads to the wilderness, to the desert, to the salty place where no one lives, out of the presence of God and His sanctuary. The fruit of God was, is, and will always be a throne of glory set up high. But how does a wicked deceitful heart get there?

The fourth and final section (Jer 17:13) answers this question. It is a call to choose the right path back to God by using an indirect analogy to the commonly known practice of ritual cleansing in a Mikveh. A mikveh is a ritual immersion pool that serves the purpose of cleansing someone for any ritual activity.[^32] This idea is first found in Lev. 15:13, which defines living water (rivers, springs, lakes, seas, or any naturally running body of water) as the type of water needed for ritual purity.[^33] Later, rabbinical tradition ranked the types of waters that could be used for ritual purity from the least preferable to the best: (1) Water in ponds, (2) water of dripping rain collected in cisterns, (3) a pool of water with forty *seah*[^34]*s,* (4) a spring of standing water, (5) a spring of running water, and finally, the best one (6) living water. [^35]

Interestingly, the word **מִקְוֶה** **mikveh** does not only mean collection of water. It is a complex word used in several meanings. It has the same root as sanctuary מִקְּדָשׁ miqq<sup>e</sup>dâsh and can mean: (1) hope, something waited for with confidence. (2) A collection of water, caravan, drove, a congregation. (3) Abiding, gathering together, weaving of a linen yarn. Understanding these complex words compels the reader to look into the original languages and find an inclusio within Lev. 17:13. Adonai, the **mikveh** of Israel … the **mikveh of living water.** Adonai himself is the mikveh of living water and those who have forsaken Adonai will be cursed with shame, written in the sand to be forgotten. Why? Because they traded off the mikveh of living water for a mikveh of broken cisterns (Jer. 2:13). In the same way Christopher Wrigth concludes:

“The verbal echoes build the links clearly. *Those who turn away from you* (13) will become like the one *whose heart turns away from the Lord* (5), and will face the same dry and dusty fate. By implication, those who do not *forsake the Lord* will have the abundant water supply not only of *a tree planted by the water* (8), but of *the spring of living water* that is the Lord himself (13; cf. 2:13).” [^36]

## **THEOLOGICAL ANALYSIS (1 page)**

Jer. 17:5-13 as shown in the text's explanation, is a deep dip into theological concepts. The main one is faith, which will bring us back to the Sanctuary of God, to His eternal presence. Jeremiah shows how Adam placed his faith in the flesh and looked for a way to follow his own will. This drove them to be like a bush in the desert instead of a tree by the streams (garden). But God has always provided a way to be cleansed and trust in the promised seed. This is the seed of grace, the seed of the gospel, the seed of thought that is eventually recovered when the actual seed of the woman comes. Salvation comes by faith in the Son (Seed) of God, who came through the woman and died so that sin would be covered. The fruit of grace is a life full of faith and hope with no shame or fear. God is sovereign, God is good, and God has only one plan since the beginning.

Deuteronomy 29 and 30 could be seen as a commentary on this main event of the garden, projecting it to the future, a future that Jeremiah is actually living. The way of death is to trust in man, and the way of life is to trust in God. The sacrifices were never meant to be for salvation, but a means to show the faith in He who was to come and die a gustatory death, just like Issac was saved, every sacrifice was intended to remind Israel of that day and pointed forward to the day of redemption. When Israel stopped trusting in God, they were exiled, but God promised to circumcise their hearts upon their return. How? Through the washing of sins and pouring of living water. Through the only hope, the only mikveh, Adonai. Jeremiah, according to Thomson, “recognized that Josiah’s reforms were in reality a retrograde movement because they threatened to undo the work of the prophets. Reformation in worship without reformation of heart was useless” [^37]

What is the path man can take to return to God’s rule? There is only one way, truth, and life: Jesus Christ, the seed that crushed the serpent on the cross and rose from death. He is the real Mikveh, the only hope and the only cleanser. The only one worthy enough to change our deceitful heart into His heart by putting the law in our hearts through the Holy Spirit. The search for the seed is over and it is now time for the resolution. The Son of God stood on the cross so everyone could look at Him and recognize the coming seed. Whoever trusts in Him will have eternal life. Whoever trusts in man will be cursed as the serpent was. For those who trust, a Sanctuary set up high, a throne of glory is waiting.

## **APPLICATION (1 page)**

In ministry and life: Choosing the right path. It is not always easy to choose the right path. Even when someone knows their heart is deceitful, they can be deceived by it. The only real application is that all who trust in the Lord actually run to the Lord. That, in a sense, every living being can be washed by the spring of living water. There is an interesting event in the life of Jesus that can illustrate how this can be applied practically.

When Jesus was about to go to the cross, he washed His disciples' feet. Peter tries to stop Him, but Jesus insists that He must wash his feet. Peter, being Peter, then asked to be washed fully instead. Jesus responds: “He who has bathed has no need to wash, except the feet; he is completely clean. And you all are clean (Jn. 13:10)” Even the ones who have been bathed have to wash their feet because they are still walking in a corrupted world. Reading and letting the Word examine our hearts and souls is like letting Jesus wash our feet with living water. He has already cleansed us, but we must wash our feet daily. Trusting in the Lord is like letting Jesus wash our feet daily through the reading and applying of His word.

Taking some principles out of Jer. 17:5-13 can show us how to do it. First, echo the past. There is a need to understand what went wrong or what went right. There is a need to dig up the foundational truths so that the big picture is revealed. Secondly, be confronted by reality by transporting the past to the present. What would that mean for the contemporary reader? Finally, remember there is a destiny and make decisions according to the destiny shown by the Word. What is the fruit of the actions the reader is taking and how would that action better reflect the character of God?

**CONCLUSION (1/2 page)**

It can be concluded that Jeremiah was an extraordinary poet. Yes, he was a tragic figure who wrestled with the message he had to proclaim. Yes, a poet who felt deeply in his soul and lamented over Israel. But is it not every poet a weeping poet? Is it not that same characteristic that makes them so great? Take, for example, Romeo and Juliet. They were tragic figures who ended in tragic destinies but are remembered as the greatest of romantics.

Jeremiah is the greatest of the poetic prophets. He intertwines the theological truths revealed from the beginning of time like no one before him. He emotionally displays those truths to engrave them in the minds of his readers. He pushes them to their final destinies, offering hope for those who trust in God and despair for those who do not. He offers the only great solution be cleansed through the true Mikveh.

# Naked but not Ashamed: Genesis 3

- Author: Daniel Lira Serhan (https://danielliraserhan-rgb.github.io/)
- Type: Exegetical paper
- Course: THEO-5307 · Dallas Baptist University
- Presented to: Dr. Jon Choi
- Date: 2024-10-13
- URL: https://danielliraserhan-rgb.github.io/ensayos/naked-but-not-ashamed/
- PDF: https://danielliraserhan-rgb.github.io/ensayos/naked-but-not-ashamed.pdf
- Language: en

*Full text of the paper, reproduced exactly as in the original document.*

---

NAKED BUT NOT ASHAMED

THE FRUIT OF SIN COVERED BY GOD’S GRACE

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

An Exegetical Paper

Presented to

Dr. Jon Choi

Dallas Baptist University

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

In Partial Fulfillment

of the Requirements for THEO-5307

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

by

Daniel Lira Serhan

October 13, 2024

TABLE OF CONTENTS

INTRODUCTION

EXEGETICAL ANALYSIS

Historical Context

Literary Context

Explanation of the Text

THEOLOGICAL ANALYSIS

CONTEMPORARY APPLICATION

CONCLUSION

BIBLIOGRAPHY

---

## INTRODUCTION

Waking up in the middle of a classroom naked is a common nightmare, at least in the West, that provokes fear and shame. But that was not always the case; Gen. 2:25[^1] portrays the days when humans could be naked but not ashamed. A time when God looked at His creation and said everything was good. Why, then, are we full of shame and fear? What had to happen so that in the present age, humans are full of shame and fear? It is evident, from this simple reality, that we live in a corrupted creation far from God’s intended design.

Lost are the days when the heavens, earth, and everything in them were good. Lost are the days when humans could run around naked but not ashamed. This paper will explore and aim to answer those questions through Genesis 3, linking shame and fear as the fruit of sin. This paper will show the contrast between God's response to sin and humans' response to sin and bring light to the present corrupted state of the world and the future living hope of God, where humans can maybe run again, naked but not ashamed.

## EXEGETICAL ANALYSIS

### Historical Context

According to tradition and scripture, Moses is the author of the Pentateuch, including the book of Genesis. Debates surrounding its authorship do not have sufficient weight to raise doubts about the general attribution to Moses[^2].  The analyzed text is Genesis 3; the narrated story has no relevant historical context other than the creation account itself.  Instead, we can look at Moses’ historical context to understand the purpose of the book and, later, the purpose of the text.

Written by Moses within the days of the exodus account, Genesis is written for the Tribes of Israel leaving Egypt. Its purpose is to reveal God’s character in contrast to the ancient Near Eastern myths[^3] and to fill the historical base for the Pentateuch and Covenants[^4]. Several ancient Near Eastern myths parallel the creation, the flood, and other Genesis accounts, but there are no parallel myths or stories about the fall, which is the center of this paper. Without the account of Genesis 3, we would not have an explanation of what went wrong with creation. Without Moses' account, we would only have myths, speculations, and vane philosophies to inform us about the origins and corruption of this world. Without Genesis, we would be in the dark, with insufficient knowledge of fundamental truths.[^5]

This paper will explore the theological focus on the covenant foundation of Gen. 3:15 more than the historical base. This text is the first mention of a coming hero, savior, or redeemer, known as the Proto-Evangelion.[^6] From this moment forward, humanity is driven by the search or wait for the redeemer to come, driving humanity's history forward.

### Literary Context

Genesis 3 precedes and continues the narrative from Genesis 2. As Sanford, Hubbard, and Bush argue, both Genesis 1 and Genesis 2 communicate the idea that “humankind is the apex of God’s creation[^7].” Genesis 2 recounts the creation in a narrative story, emphasizing the creation of humanity as the center. Genesis 3 narrates how this Apex behaved and brought about corruption to God’s Design. All three chapters constitute one big message that sets the stage for the bible narrative:

God created everything, and it was good. He made humans so that He could walk among them and they could delight in Him. Something went wrong, and this design was corrupted. From here on, the bible is the express character of God revealing Himself, His purpose, and His redeeming plan through the covenants. Genesis 3 is the key that unlocks bible interpretation by telling us what went wrong and how it will be fixed.

It is important to note that Gen. 3:1 begins with waw (וְ), a coordinating conjunction that unites two ideas. This denotes a connection with, at least, the last verse from Genesis 2, setting up the stage for the narrative of Genesis 3. Gen. 2:25 communicates God’s uncorrupted design, naked but not ashamed. At the same time, in Genesis 3, as Sanford, Hubbard, and Bush said, “we hear an exquisite, literary narrative, almost a drama”[^8] on how this design became corrupted by human intervention. Considering this verse before analyzing Genesis 3 is crucial.[^9] Naked but not ashamed becomes the main pattern representing humans’ corrupted identity after the first time they disobey God.

Following Genesis 3, we find a subsequent pattern of Genealogies that follows the destinies of the descendants of Adam and Eve.[^10] Genesis 3-11 describes a spiral of decadence on the corrupted identity and design and how this corruption expanded to siblings, to the earth and everything in it, and finally to the nations. This is the result of the events in Genesis 3. Genesis 12 picks up on the promise God made in Genesis 3:15 and begins revealing God’s plan of redemption through Abram’s seed.

Given the fundamental aspect of this chapter, it is paramount to understand what happened to God’s “good” design to comprehend the world’s present age condition and humans’ new corrupted identity: naked and ashamed. As explained in the paper, this identity is the fruit of sin (seed of the serpent), producing a pattern of behavior in response to sin. Contrasting Adam’s actions, God solves the problem by providing a better way to be covered, reversing the consequences of sin and birthing a new pattern of behavior representing the seed of the woman and a faith-based relation to God.

This paper will highlight the contrast based on these words: 1) Naked but not ashamed vis a vis Naked and ashamed. 2) Fruit of sin vis a vis fruit of grace.

### Explanation of the Text

The setting where Genesis 3 begins is the garden, where the man and his wife are naked but not ashamed. With a play of words, the text introduces a new character, the serpent, described only by one adjective: the shrewdest beast in the field.[^11] The adjective describing the serpent carries a negative connotation, as seen by the question asked of the woman, which seems to twist the character of God by overemphasizing strictness. In an analysis based on the Septuagint and other Greek translations, Fausset and Brown note that “others have more approximately translated it \[by πανονργος\], skilled in all manner of deceit and mischief.”[^12]  Rendering then, the adjective “shrewd” with a negative connotation—a master in the art of deceit and dishonor.

Furthermore, analyzing the original Hebrew will highlight an intentional play of words that shed light on the contrast in the text. The Hebrew word for shrewd, עָרוּם (*ʿārûm),* has the same root and is parallel to the word for naked עָרוֹם (*ʿārôm*) [^13] in Gen. 2:25 and nakedness in Gen. 3:7 עֵרֹם (*ʿêrōm)*.[^14] This provides our first hint to the patterns revealed in Genesis 3. The text’s first intention is to introduce a character described in direct relation to the man's and his wife's identity and design.

The innocent, unashamed nakedness (*ʿārôm*) would meet the dishonoring, shameful shrewdness (*ʿārûm)* of the serpent who twists the words of God, generating doubt in the woman’s heart.

The serpent presents a character of God with an overly strict sense of rules—one who prohibits everything (Gen. 3:1). The woman was probably full of doubt, as she most certainly knew His creator and had enjoyed the fruit of other trees. In a sense, trying to defend God, the woman falls into the trap and makes her first mistake. She engages the serpent and lets the serpent know about her weaknesses. Her answer agrees with the serpent’s question but, to a lower degree, “you must not touch it.” A degree of strictness that was not originally there, misrepresenting God and giving the serpent a chance to continue its deceit. (Gen 3:2-3).[^15] Could it be that those words added were not even hers? Could it be that she heard those from Adam? This might only be speculation, but what is true is that the direct command was given to Adam. His responsibility was to correct those mistakes.

When the serpent saw that Adam did not intervene and that the woman’s answer contained a slight mistake, it continued its mischief. Gen. 2:4 is the serpent's bold move, a direct lie, an opposition to God, a direct challenge to His honor, authority, and character: “You most assuredly would not die.” This lie was coupled with a sweet promise: “You will be like God” (Gen. 2:5). The serpent’s craftiness presents a twofold lie: eliminating consequences sweetened by the possibility of being like God. A half-truth supported this twofold lie; their eyes would be open, and in a way, they would be like God: “Knowing good and evil.”

Knowing good and evil will only serve one purpose: abandoning God. This was the true temptation. Knowledge about what is good and what is bad offers the capability of discerning and thus governing oneself—the idea of being free of others who might know better.[^16] This is the foundation of all sin: Deciding to dishonor God by dishonoring His commands while believing it could be done better.

Once again, the woman fell into the trap, this time forgetting God and giving in to her desires—desires that show the woman's increasing fall into temptation. Gen. 3:6 shows her thought process and how it went from shallow as any white lie to deep and as dark as shrewdness. “Food” was something easy to accept. “Lust for the eyes” was more profound and troublesome. It spoke directly to being able to see like God. But seeing is a passive action that would not create any harm. Finally, the desire to “impart wisdom.” Having convinced herself that she wanted the fruit and its “innocent” benefits, her mind traveled to the logical next step, using that knowledge to rule without needing God.

She took, she gave, and he ate. Adam was there all along and did not stop her. He did not take the necessary responsibility for what God gave him to rule (Gen. 3:6). The serpent's seed of lies gave fruit. Just like it said, their eyes opened, but the first thing they saw was עֵרֹם (*ʿêrōm).* They were both naked, but this time, they felt shame. Their response was to cover themselves to cover their shame. (Gen 3:7). The innocent, unashamed nakedness meets the deceitful seed of the serpent, producing the fruit of shame and the response of humans, self-covering.

Their eyes were opened, stripping them of their innocence, dishonoring God, and perverting His design—now the man and his wife are naked and ashamed. Shame is the first fruit of sin; without God’s intervention, shame will always produce self-covering. God’s design got corrupted, and nakedness and shrewdness became entangled. From this point on, all through the Bible, the word naked or nakedness in their different Hebrew variations (*ʿārôm*, *ʿêrōm*, *ʿeryâ*, *ʿerwâ*, *maʿar*, *maʿ*<sup>*a*</sup>*rōm*, *yāḏ*[^17]) carry a negative connotation of being dishonored, exposed, bare, stripped. It even carries sexual connotations such as lust, intercourse, and incest. All these variations are associated directly with shame, the fruit of sin.

The second fruit of sin is shown in Gen. 3:8. As they cover themselves, they discern they have done evil in the eyes of God. Having now a distorted idea of God’s character, they became full of fear and hid themselves. Fear is the second fruit of sin, and humans respond to it by hiding or alienating themselves. Both shame and fear are the fruit of sin, meaning they were born out of sin and then, in themselves, produce a pattern of behavior, self-covering and hiding from God. Without God’s intervention, humans will always be ruled by shame and fear of others and God. But God does intervene right away. He shows his real character and responds in complete contrast to the response of men. He goes out of His way to find them and extend an opportunity to speak (Gen 3:9).

In the same way, the serpent had approached them with words, God now approached them to speak with them. Within this conversation, God exposed their fear and shame through questions, but not with the same intention as the serpent (Gen 3:10-11). He did so with his hand stretched with grace. Instead of dying immediately, Adam and his wife spoke with God, revealing God’s relational nature. Through those questions, the patterns of shame and fear reveal themselves. Adam tries to cover himself by blaming God and his wife (Gen 3:12). The woman tries to cover herself by blaming the serpent (Gen 3:13), and the serpent had no choice; it was the perpetrator and fully knew what it was doing.

What transpires next within Gen. 3:14-20 is the most beautiful display of God’s response: the seed of God’s grace that gives the fruit of faith and living hope. Buried between the lines of apparent judgment, the author, inspired by the Holy Spirit, displays God’s grace and introduces the blessed hope in which faith is placed. God addresses the story's three characters in the order in which they appear and decrees judgment on each. Within each of the judgments, the text reveals God’s grace.

The serpent, He curses, ( אָר֤וּר *ʾârar*) (Gen. 3:14). [^18] This is the first mention of the word “cursed,” it is essential to understand its meaning from this context to project it onto later texts. To do so, the context and the underlying motivation of the action against God should be considered. The original command and its consequences provide the context: The penalty of sin, of rebelling against God, was death. The motivation or temptation brought forward by the serpent and accepted by both the man and his wife was self-ruling. Death and self-ruling should be intertwined to accurately describe the word cursed *(ʾârar)* and its subsequent variations. Cursed as in separated from God’s rule, left to its own and destined for destruction. [^19]

This can be further understood by the consequences applied to the serpent. In Genesis 1, God created creatures that could walk, swim, or fly, and he looked at His creation and said it was good. According to Genesis 3:14, the serpent would be “separated” from all the earth's creatures by a specific trait: its locomotion. As Hess would explain, “… the mode of locomotion for the serpent is one which is characteristic of those creatures who are unclean. They do not walk nor swim nor fly.”[^20] In a sense, God separated the serpent from all His creation, leaving it on its own and destined for destruction. This destruction would come in the hands of a hero, the woman’s seed.

Gen. 3:15 is a foundational verse that explains the main plotline to be traced throughout God’s revelation and human history.[^21] Animosity will sprout between the woman and the serpent, between the woman’s seed (זַרְעֲ *zeraʿ*) and the serpent’s seed (זַרְעֲ *zeraʿ*). The serpent and the woman will be forever against each other, and their seeds will be at war until the woman’s seed (*zeraʿ*) crushes the head of the serpent’s seed. The judgment of the serpent became a promise to humanity.

The woman's seed (*zeraʿ*) is the promised hero, while the serpent's seed becomes the villain. The climax is the crushing of its head, and the motif behind it becomes God’s grace. As in any story, tracing the hero reveals the plot, and tracing the word seed (*zeraʿ*) becomes of uttermost importance. Israel’s history is driven by the search for the redeemer to come and the patterns of animosity against the enemy who wants to destroy her and her offspring. Where does this seed come from? For Adam and his wife, it was implied that the seed came from both. But, the careful words of God tell a different story: from the woman will come the seed (*zeraʿ).*

The woman is not cursed, and God does not even condemn any action. It might be implied that her actions are not as deliberate as the serpents nor as rebellious as his husband, who directly disobeyed. She did participate, so God does not mention her actions directly but does judge.[^22] The idea of self-ruling became the basis of her consequences. God places two consequences on the woman. First, that which was given to her as a gift, conception to labor, will cause pain (עִצָּבוֹן֙). Secondly, knowing her desire was to be self-ruled, she would now be limited in authority, given that her husband would rule over her (Gen. 3:16). This would mark women’s purpose and struggle: to give birth in pain and to be ruled not directly by God, but by man under God.

The man is not cursed, but the ground is cursed because of him. God condemns two of his actions, listening to his wife and eating from the Trea. Listening to His wife was not directly a rebellion against God. Instead, it showed a lack of appreciation for His design and letting what he was responsible for become corrupted. His direct action of disobeying God and eating the tree is also condemned and deserves a curse: death. In an act of God’s grace, what was cursed was not him but the ground he was placed to rule over.[^23] The ground is taken out of God's rule and doomed to be ruled by men, a ruling that will cause corruption and destruction (Gen. 3:17). God’s grace did not exempt Adam from consequences. In the same way that a woman’s primary purpose causes pain, now Adams’s purpose causes pain (עֶצֶב). As it is now cursed and corrupted, the ground will give man hardship to labor in (Gen.18-19). Both accounts are linked by the same Hebrew root (עֶצֶב ʿetseb), meaning both consequences carry the same weight even when their actions are different. Their primary purpose, design, and identity are now corrupted and will cause pain.

The judgment may seem harsh, but a closer would show that Genesis 3:14-19 displays God’s grace. Adam and his wife deserved death but obtained a seed of grace that would give fruit. Adam’s answer to God is to change his wife's name to Eve, “the mother of all living” (Gen. 3:20).  This reflects that both Adam and Eve had faith. They both believed, trusted and accepted what God said he would do[^24]. They placed their faith in the seed, their living hope for the coming one. God then provided them a better covering, “made out of skin,” to remove their shame and fear. Where did this skin come from? The first sacrifice ever made. The payment for sin was death, and death did happen. God used this sacrifice to cover them from their shame and provided their new identity: Covered and not ashamed (Gen. 3:21).

Finally, the actual result of eating the tree is “the man has become like one of Us, knowing good and evil” (Gen 3:22). There is much debate about what the meaning of Us would be. Be it the trinity or a divine counsel of divine beings. What should not be confused is that man did not become fully like God. The grammar indicates that man became like God in the characteristic of knowing good and evil. This knowing gives the capacity to discern and make decisions without considering God as the higher authority, but it does not give man the capability to choose good over evil.[^25] As such, God protected them by expelling them from the sight of the Tree of Life. He then placed cherubim to guard the Tree so they would not eat and live corrupted forever.

## THEOLOGICAL ANALYSIS

Gen. 3 gives the foundation of the plotline for the book of Genesis and shows the patterns to look for. Based on this chapter, Genesis 4-11 explores the pattern of both seeds’ genealogies and their animosity[^26]. The seed of the woman is those who still invoke the Name of the Lord (Genesis 4), while the serpent's seed is those who always choose evil. Eventually, the text shows that when given a chance, humans will choose evil. Regardless of their condition, God is faithful, and tracing the seed of women leads the text to Abram’s election and promises (Genesis 12, 15, 17). The latter part of the book of Genesis, Genesis 12-50, is to be understood in light of Genesis 3 as the genealogy of the seed to come, rendering Israel the woman who births the seed.[^27] As it began, Genesis once finishes with a promise of a ruler that will come to take what belongs to Him: “The scepter will not pass from Judah, nor the ruler’s staff from between his feet, until he to whom it belongs will come. To him will be the obedience of the peoples (Gen 49:10).

The animosity between the woman and the serpent drives Israel’s history, and the people choose to be ruled by God or man. Seeing this pattern opens up the understanding of prophecy. Tracing the seed of the serpent will render insight into prophesies and the seven kingdoms that were a part of its influence. Egypt, Assyria, Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, Rome, and the empire of the last days (Revelation 13).

From Genesis 3, we learn that the fruit of sin corrupted man's identity creating shame and fear. But by God’s grace, there is a way to be covered, and it comes through faith and the birth of everlasting hope. This is the seed of grace, the seed of the gospel, the seed of thought that is eventually recovered when the actual seed of the woman comes. Salvation comes by faith in the Son (Seed) of God, who came through the woman and died so that sin would be covered. The fruit of grace is a life full of faith and hope with no shame or fear. God is sovereign, God is good, and God has only one plan since the beginning. The seed to come was always to be the Son of God incarnate. The one that was to come through the line of Judah came. He is the only human that can sustain a life of complete submission to the Father because he is not just a man, but He is both human and divine in nature, the Son of God, the seed of the woman. This salvation has always come and will always come by believing in the seed promised in Genesis 3:15.

What is the path man can take to return to God’s rule? There is only one way, truth, and life: Jesus Christ, the seed that crushed the serpent on the cross and rose from death, making a spectacle of him. The search for the seed is over, the story's climax has been reached, and it is now time for the resolution. The Son of God stood on the cross so everyone could look at Him and recognize the coming seed. Whoever clings to the seed will have eternal life. Whoever clings to themselves will be cursed as the serpent was.

The root of sin is rebellion, being out of God’s rule, and the fruit of sin will always provoke shame and fear. This truth can be traced throughout the Bible. Shame and fear are then synonyms for fear of man. Acting because of shame or fear will always produce dissatisfaction and corruption. The root of grace is the return to God’s rule, and the fruit of grace is faith, which overcomes fear and clothes with a new identity. An identity of a son of God, redeemed by the Son and sealed by the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 1).

An authentic human response to suffering must always retain an element of protest against suffering which cannot be justified. Hence the autocratic God of absolute power who simply presides over this suffering world and cannot himself be reached by suffering appears a cosmic monster. It seems possible to justify God (‘theodicy’) only if he too suffers. ‘The only credible theology for Auschwitz is one that makes God an inmate of the place.’<sup>8</sup>[^28]<sup>0</sup>[^29]

## CONTEMPORARY APPLICATION

Since shame and fear began after the fall, they can be used as a thermometer to indicate how far away someone has drifted from God’s authority. It works on a personal level, in a group setting, for a state, a country, or even the world of this present age. A quick review of this world will show that the underlying motivation for everything that goes on in the world is shame and fear. Adam and Eve self-covered with fig leaves and hid from God. Today, society covers their shame in gender identity, in complete nakedness and exposure, redefining what is good and evil. Men and women who are terrified of the responsibility of other humans hide behind planned parenthood.  A husband who does not know how to raise their kids covers his shame in violence. High schoolers cover their shame by being one more in the group and falling into social pressure. A damaged kid hides his fear by overcompensating. One way or another, everyone is hiding and covering for themselves.[^30]

Noticing shame and fear can lead pastors, lay leaders, or friends to approach the affected like God did, gracefully asking questions to produce a confession that leads to repentance. Leaders should always follow up by reminding others that the shame felt will only be covered by the blood of Christ and that God is not one to punish but one who approaches with patience and love. Looking at the world with Genesis 3 in mind should lead the believer to always look for the underlying motivation for someone’s action. If it is a shame, then they should show them how God covers all sin. If it is fear, then they should show them how God’s heart is gentle and humble. By doing so, the root of the problem may be solved, and what once was sin could be met with grace and produce faith in the living God.

Christ did pray: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Lk. 23:34). It is only by the Father's forgiveness that we can be covered. What is then for a man to do? Understand that the root of all sin is rebellion. Once someone has rebelled, they stop looking for God’s authority, and without it, every action will eventually lead to fear and shame. How could a church prioritize covering shame and fear? What could it look like? What programs should it have? How would it share the gospel?

Teenagers live in a world surrounded by shame; they need figures who can ground them to their true identity. Young adults live with the fear of not being able to provide or of not living up to the world’s expectations; they need to be reminded that God provides and that he is already satisfied at the moment one is born again. Young adults live in the shame of not finding a partner to create a life and a family, with the fear they will never do; they need someone in a community that lifts their eyes and joins them in creating something for the community, reminding them that God is our first relation and is sufficient to provide. Adult men live with the shame of not being like the next one and the fear of being unable to bring bread to the table; they need a community of men that empowers them to live life emulating Christ.

Church members, in whatever role they play, could become a community that detects shame and exposes it for what it truly is, then gracefully provide the covering that erases all shame. A community that detects when someone is hiding gracefully searches for them and leads them back to God, who protects them. A community that walks covered and not ashamed.

## CONCLUSION

Genesis 3 is the key that unlocks everything. It is the gospel in its simplest form. It explains what went wrong, when it went wrong and how it will be fixed. According to God’s design, there should be no shame or fear; the original design was meant to be naked but not ashamed.

After Adam and Eve fell from God’s rule, He searched for them, He spoke to them, He judged them, He covered them, and He protected them. Within it all, He promised a seed would come and crush the head of the serpent, ending the fruit of sin once and for all. Wherever men think they can converse themselves, God can do it better. Wherever men believe they can hide, God will always find them. But when he does, he does not curse but provides a way for confession and repentance.

This is His grace delivered to Adam and Eve, which sprouted faith and hope in the seed to come and the age to come. This is His grace delivered for every human being, that through Christ, they can be covered and walk without shame. It is the living hope that one day His children can be resurrected and walk once more: naked but not ashamed.

# In Christ: For the Praise of His Glory

- Author: Daniel Lira Serhan (https://danielliraserhan-rgb.github.io/)
- Type: Exegetical paper
- Course: THEO · Dallas Baptist University
- Presented to: Dr. Brent Thomason
- Date: 2025-04-26
- URL: https://danielliraserhan-rgb.github.io/ensayos/in-christ/
- PDF: https://danielliraserhan-rgb.github.io/ensayos/in-christ.pdf
- Language: en

---

“In Christ”

For The Praise of His Glory

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

An Exegetical Paper

Presented to

Dr. Brent Thomason

Dallas Baptist University

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

In Partial Fulfillment

of the Requirements for THEO-

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

by

Daniel Lira Serhan

April 26, 2025

TABLE OF CONTENTS

INTRODUCTION

CONTEXT

CONTENT

APPLICATION

CONCLUSION

BIBLIOGRAPHY

---

## INTRODUCTION

An essential question arises in every human being, regardless of race, religion, or culture. This question has baffled philosophers and thinkers. A question that every Human being is compelled to ask and try to answer. What is the purpose of life? What is a human being? And

Once the first question is answered, as every religion and philosophy does, the question then shifts from a foundational “why” to a practical “how.” How can someone accomplish their purpose? What is the plan to achieve it, and how does an individual’s life fit into that plan? In Christian terms, it is shown as the heavily coveted “calling.

The focus of this paper is to show that the church is built upon *the work of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit*, contained “in Christ” to **The Praise of His Glory.** To do so, it will explore Ephesians 1:1-14 to show how Paul answers these questions by pointing to God's purpose for all things, and how in their perfect condition, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit collaborate in unity to fulfill that purpose and give the foundation for the church “In Christ”.

## CONTEXT

**Letter to the Ephesians**

A letter written by Paul while in prison in Rome (Acts 28:16), probably around 60 AD, aims to lay the foundations for the church. In this paper, the word church is not used as a specific congregation but rather implies the saints, both jew and gentile, comprising the different communities and the global body of Christ. Some of the oldest texts do not contain the phrase “in Ephesus,” as it was intended to be a circular letter circulated among the churches in the region[^1]. It was not a reactive letter, such as Paul would predominantly write; instead, it clarifies a message to the church that began predominantly Jewish and is now becoming predominantly Gentile, reminding them of the Jewish apocalyptic framework of this era, the coming era, and the role of the church in this reality.

As such, it establishes the basis for what the church is built upon (theology), what the church is and does (missiology), and how the church functions (practical). This three-fold idea gives the main structure to the letter: Ephesians 1 and 2 focus primarily on building the church upon Who God is, what He did, why He did it, and what He has purposed for the church. Ephesians 3 and 4 transition into how the church impacts the building up of the church and pushes its mission forward. Finally, Ephesians 5 and 6 show how this reality and this mission affect our daily lives.

CONTENT

**Salutation: ἐν Χριστός (“In Christ”)**

The letter is addressed to the saints, whom it describes as those faithful “In Christ.” The use of the preposition **ἐν** within the phrase “in Christ” should stop the reader as an apparent grammatical incoherence. It should be expected to find a preposition that denotes the object of faith, such as “to” in any of its Greek variants. Instead, Paul uses **ἐν,** a preposition that denotes the position of the faithful rather than an object of faith.[^2] By doing so, Paul is defining the faithful, the church, as those contained, inside of, positioned in, belonging within, clothed by, “in Christ”.

In the next thirteen verses, Paul uses the same phrase with a slight variation a total of eleven times. For this reason, it is within this salutation that Paul provides the key to understanding the letter of Ephesians, specifically, the theology that lays the foundation of the church. As Keathley notes, “Paul’s repeated use of the term reveals that it is the central key to the apostle’s doctrine of salvation and perhaps even his whole theology.” Just like one hops into an ark, Paul describes salvation as being “in Christ,” placing Jesus as the container of the Church destined for salvation.

Union with Christ is the core truth of salvation that can be seen either as encompassing all of salvation or as the center to which all components of salvation are connected.[^3]

The primary identity of the church is a position “in Christ” and not a function, it is a gift and not an achievement, it is a union with Christ in every aspect. Life. Elected “in Christ”, participants of His life, death, and resurrection “in Christ,” partakers of every blessing “in Christ, and destined for eternal life “in Christ. Paul states that “in Adam all die, even so in Christ all shall be made alive” (1 Cor 15:22).[^4]

**The Blessing of The Father, The Son, and The Holy Spirit “in Christ”**

The next eleven verses are a single sentence in the Greek original recited as a Jewish blessing. [^5] Having stressed the Church’s union “in Christ”, Paul uses this blessing to show the church is built for **The Praise of His Glory** upon *the work of the three Persons of the Trinity*[^6]. The adoption from the Father, the redemption from the Son, and the seal from the Holy Spirit are presented by Paul both as a doxology (**The Praise of His Glory**) and as the basic identity of the faithful saints “In Christ” [^7]. Meaning that each person of the Trinity gives **Praise to The Glory of God** (doxology) through an action that builds the church.

**The doxology of the Father Ephesians 1:3-6**

The first section of the benediction is the doxology offered from the Father to the God-head through the adoption of the church. Now that the church is “In Christ,” it has received every blessing in the heavenly places. While it does benefit the church, the main purpose of *the work of the Father* is **The Praise of His Glor**y.

The Father’s maximum offering of **Praise for His glory** is accomplished by (1) blessing the church “in Christ”, (2) choosing the church “in Christ” before the foundation of the world to be holy, and (3) pre-destining it to adoption through Christ as His children. For simplicity's sake, *the work of the Father* can be summarized as the adoption of the church “in Christ”.

Paul reinforces the concept of being “in Christ” as the container of the blessings received from the Father. In Him, the church is chosen, predestined, and elected for love and adoption. To explain the concept, Paul takes the reader back to the beginning. Even before creation, the Father loved the church, but He did it through Christ and “in Christ” alone. The container is predestined, so the saints receive their predestination only when in the container itself. Akin notes “Paul supplies the answer: we were elected in Christ Jesus. God elected his own Son, who is our representative, and we find our election in him.”[^8]

The saints can benefit from the doxology of the Father, knowing that their true identity is as sons, not by any accomplishment, but by the goodness and love of the Father. He loved by His own choice. He did not need to do it, yet He still did it. The plan was established before the creation of the world. He decided beforehand to adopt the saints “in Christ”. Knowing what would have to happen the Father devised the perfect plan through Christ and in Christ. Kesner explains how the church's identity is changed and now both Israel and the Church are children of God. “People remained with their cultural identity, but through *the work of Messiah*, their legal status has changed to become the spiritual children of God.[^9]

*The work of the Father* is the adoption of the saints **for the Praise of His Glory.**

**The doxology of the Son Ephesians 1:7-12**

The second section of the benediction is the doxology offered from the Son to the Godhead through the redemption of the church. As noted earlier, the adoption is not only “in Christ” but also through Christ. As such, *the work of the Son* makes the adoption possible by redeeming the saints through the removal of their trespasses by His blood. It is worth noting again that while the saints do benefit, the main purpose of *the work of the Son* is **the praise of His glory.**

The Son’s maximum offering of **Praise for His glory** is accomplished by (1) redemption “in Christ” through His blood, (2) giving of His Grace in abundance as an inheritance “in Christ”, and (3) the revealing of the mystery of His will “in Christ”. For simplicity's sake, *the work of the Son* can be summarized as the redemption of the church “in Christ” and through Christ.

In this section, Paul explains how the plan devised beforehand is carried out through Christ for the redemption of the saints. Meaning, the deliverance from bondage of sin and the acquisition of the saints for eternal inheritance “in Christ”.[^10] While doing so, the Son revealed the eternal plan devised, according to Hoehner,  “not out of but according to (*kata*) the wealth of His grace.[^11] The unveiling of this plan is indeed the unveiling of the Son as The Christ and as such it is the eternal “plan (**ŏikŏnŏmia)**[^12] of the fullness of times is to bring all things together in the Messiah—both things in heaven and things on earth, all in Him.” (Eph 1:10)

Once more, Paul takes the reader back to the beginning. In Adam, the task given to humankind to (**ŏikŏnŏmia**) steward and rule the land and everything in it, is corrupted. However, God beforehand had predestined that “in Christ” all things would be united for a good (**ŏikŏnŏmia**) stewardship in the fullness of time.

The saints can benefit from the doxology of the Son by knowing they have been redeemed, bought by the precious blood of Christ for an eternal inheritance.[^13] But also by understanding the eternal plan to put everything under the feet of Christ for a correct rulership and ass such surrendering today everything to Him.

*The work of the Son* is the redemption of the saints **for the Praise of His Glory.**

**The Doxology of The Holy Spirit Ephesians 1:13-14**

The third section of the benediction is the doxology offered from the Holy Spirit to the Godhead by sealing the church “in Christ,” given that the saints are adopted by the Father and redeemed by the Son for an inheritance. The Holy Spirit then “seals” the promise as a down payment of what is to come. Once more, while the saints benefit, the main purpose of *the work of the Holy Spirit* is **the praise of His glory.**

The Holy Spirit’s maximum offering of **Praise for His glory** is accomplished by (1) sealing the saints “in Christ”  (2) as a guarantee of the inheritance to come (3) while still waiting for its fulfillment. For simplicity's sake, *the work of the Holy Spirit* can be summarized as the sealing of the church “in Christ”.

By being united to Christ and redeemed through Christ, the plan of adoption is fulfilled, but not yet fully received. The good news is that by hearing and believing that God saves through Christ, the saints are adopted and then sealed. Harold Heohner demonstrates that it is once more *the work of the trinity* exalting the Godhead: “God is the One who seals, Christ is the sphere in which the **seal** is done, and the Holy Spirit is the instrument of the seal.” [^14]

It should be noted that this seal is a double-fold blessing. The word used by Paul, **sphragizō**[^15]**,** implies complete ownership and security carried by the owner. According to Keener: “A wax seal would have a mark of ownership or identification stamped in it, identifying who was attesting what was inside the container that had been sealed.”[^16] The first blessing is the identification of the saints as belonging to God “in Christ.”

The second blessing can be discovered by the word **Arrhăbon**, or guarantee. In the seal of the Holy Spirit, the saints have received a guarantee of the inheritance to come. However, this is a “term used in ancient business documents to mean a ‘down payment.” It is, in itself, a bond, a sum of money, a large part of the payment, given in advance as a guarantee that the full amount will be paid later. This means that the saints, through the Holy Spirit, can live a life that testifies to themselves of the life to come in the age to come.

*The work of the Holy Spirit* is the seal of the saints **for the Praise of His Glory.**

## APPLICATION

The letter to the Ephesians is foundational for the church; as such, it should be considered in every sphere of Christian life. It is not a reactionary letter and is not to be taken to “solve” problems within the church or the believer. As such, every pastor and counselor should always take it as a solid foundation to ground the believer and the church so that they may grow into maturity and conformity to Christ. This should be done by grounding the believer in the identity provided by God “in Christ” and the purpose of all creation to **Praise the Glory of God.** By doing so, the pastor and counselor can help ensure that every aspect of the believer’s life is rightly oriented and plays a role within this era while creation waits for the fullness of time.

When confronting every life decision, the counselor and pastor should guide the believer to examine the doxology of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit and ask: If the maximum work of God was done not for the benefit of the saints but for the praise of His Glory, then what should the purpose of the saint be?  The answer is clear and straightforward: The saints are to be **for the Praise of His Glory.** This means that every decision should be passed through a filter: How is this action praising the glory of God? How does this action exhibit God’s attributes to exalt Him?

These questions could push the saints to live a life based on works. However, when analyzing *the work of the Trinity*, it should be noted that the only way to give all the praise to His glory is by living in the identity already provided “in Christ,” to rest on who He says the saints are and not on how the saints might perceive themselves. Thus, the *work of the saints* is to rest “in Christ” and represent Christ by living out their identity. Sons of God adopted by the Father, redeemed through the Son, and sealed by the Holy Spirit “in Christ.”

In every moment of doubt, disillusionment, depression, or anxiety, the saint can look back at Ephesians to be built up again in the certainty that they have been chosen, predestined, loved, sealed, bought, forgiven, and guaranteed for the age to come. At the same time, look at the “down-payment” given by the Holy Spirit as the first fruits of their own resurrection, as to live a life taking hold of eternal life.

Finally, with a deep understanding of the great mystery revealed, the church should strive to live in the present age under the authority of the king to come: the Christ in whom all things will be united in the fullness of time. Thus, the church should live a life of simple obedience to the one who blessed us for The Praise of His Glory.

## CONCLUSION

As *Kenneth Keathley* highlights: “Clearly, ‘in Christ’ is not an empty phrase, a throwaway line, or a space-filler expression to the apostle. His repetition is not a mantra. Paul’s repeated use of the term reveals that it is the central key to the apostle’s doctrine of salvation and perhaps even his whole theology.”[^17] Understanding the meaning of being united with Christ, being one with Christ, and being contained in Christ should be the foundation of Christian life. It should be the lens through which Pauline theology and even Johannine theology are read. Doing so would not only solve eternal debates about predestination, but it would also trust the believer to live a life based on an identity given as a gift and prepared beforehand.

It is “in Christ” that the saints are saved, predestined, loved, redeemed, sealed, contained, prepared, preserved, justified, empowered, covered, and blessed. As John Murray explains, “Union with Christ is a very inclusive subject. It embraces the wide span of salvation from its ultimate source in the eternal election of God to its final fruition in the glorification of the elect… Union with Christ binds all together...”[^18]

It is “in Christ” that the church can be built up. It is “in Christ” that the church can thrive. It is “in Christ” and “in Christ” alone that the saints and the church can live a life that fully gives **all the Praise to His glory.**

The church has been chosen beforehand for adoption, redemption, and sealing “in Christ” for an age to come in which Christ will steward the heavens and the earth. All was done not by the Trinity for the Praise of His Glory. May the lives of every member of the church and *the work of the saints* rest always in Christ and be for **The Praise Of His Glory.**
